analysis.one_liner: Makes oil and gas companies prove their mergers will not reduce competition.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten antitrust rules for the oil and gas industry. In any court case challenging an oil or gas industry merger, the merging companies — not the government — would have to prove the deal will not substantially lessen competition or create a monopoly. It also would have required the FTC and the Justice Department's antitrust division to rewrite their merger guidelines within six months, specifically to account for the oil market's features: demand that barely falls when prices rise, few ways for new competitors to enter, and limited refining capacity. The bill's findings blamed high gasoline and heating oil prices on a decade of mergers that concentrated the industry.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who buy gasoline, diesel, home heating oil, and natural gas. The bill was designed to make it easier to block oil and gas industry mergers, on the theory that a less consolidated industry is more competitive and charges lower prices. Its findings pointed to high prices for these everyday energy products and said the antitrust agencies had allowed a decade of consolidation to go unchecked.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of gasoline and heating fuel

how_it_helps.text: In court challenges to oil and gas industry mergers, the companies doing the merging would have to prove the deal will not substantially lessen competition or create a monopoly — reversing the usual antitrust burden of proof, under which the government must prove harm.

It would require the FTC and the Justice Department's Antitrust Division to jointly rewrite their merger enforcement guidelines within six months to specifically cover oil and gas transactions, and to account for the industry's special conditions: demand that stays strong even as prices rise, high barriers to entry, limited refining capacity, and the ease of gaining market power.

The bill's findings state that high gasoline, heating oil, and natural gas prices were caused in substantial part by a decade of mergers and acquisitions that concentrated the industry, and that antitrust agencies failed to stop it — the bill aims to restore competition in production, refining, distribution, and retail sale.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would face a heavy burden of proof for any future merger, acquisition, or transaction in the industry, making consolidation harder. Supporters acknowledged this could also block some mergers that might have produced efficiencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking to merge

drawbacks.text: Reversing the burden of proof for an entire industry is a blunt instrument: merging companies would have to prove a merger will not lessen competition rather than the government proving it will, which could block some oil mergers even when they might have produced real efficiencies or lower costs.

The bill addresses only future mergers. It does nothing to undo the consolidation that had already taken place over the prior decade, which the bill's own findings blame for the market power of the remaining companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the scales favor the bill: the bill's own findings describe an industry where demand is inelastic and entry is hard, so market power gained through consolidation is unlikely to be offset by competition, and merger cost savings in oil historically have not shown up at the pump. The real cost is a design tradeoff — reversing the burden of proof for an entire industry is a blunt instrument that would also block some mergers that might have produced genuine efficiencies, rather than letting agencies weigh those efficiencies case by case under the existing framework. The bill does nothing about consolidation that already occurred, only future transactions. Net: a defensible pro-consumer policy, though a blunt one.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: S. 878 was introduced in the Senate on March 14, 2007 by Sen. Herb Kohl, with Sen. Arlen Specter joining as a cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day.
No further action was ever recorded — no committee hearings, no markup, no floor vote — before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies came out ahead: they kept facing the ordinary antitrust standard for mergers, and the industry consolidation the bill blamed for high prices faced no added obstacles. Consumers continued to bear whatever cost that consolidation produces at the pump.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies, and continued industry consolidation

for.name: Herb Kohl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Joined Kohl in introducing the bill as its Republican cosponsor.

for.name: One Independent senator
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, one of its two cosponsors.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; no markup or vote was ever scheduled and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — a Democrat, a Republican, and an Independent cosponsored it — but the bill never reached a vote, so no record exists of how parties lined up for or against it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The bill would have made oil and gas mergers and acquisitions much harder to complete by placing the burden of proof on the merging companies and requiring stricter agency merger guidelines. Its findings tie industry consolidation to higher prices at the pump, so the industry's freedom to consolidate ran against consumers' interest in lower prices.
